item.title: Linux IPv4 TCP use-after-free
item.dc:creator: Cloudforce One
item.description: Prioritize patching. Atlas updated its distribution review to report fixed RHEL kernels and remaining vendor-specific patch gaps. Check the running host kernel against your distribution's CVE advisory, apply its fixed kernel, and complete the required reboot or vendor-supported activation procedure. Verify that the fix is active, including on container hosts and Kubernetes nodes.
item.content:encoded:
Prioritize patching · Last checked Nov 2, 2026

A race condition in Linux's IPv4 TCP connection handling can expose kernel memory, crash a host, or allow remote code execution before application authentication.

Update chronology

  • Nov 1, 2026: Atlas updated its distribution review to report fixed RHEL kernels and remaining vendor-specific patch gaps.
  • Oct 30, 2026: Red Hat published a Critical-impact bulletin and interim network-filtering guidance.
  • Oct 29, 2026: The Go Security Team published MPTCP applicability guidance, subsequently mirrored on oss-security.
  • Oct 27, 2026: Anthropic disclosed a working research exploit for remote root command execution against MPTCP listeners.
  • Oct 15, 2026: The Linux kernel CNA published the CVE record with upstream fix references.

What happened

  • CVE-2026-98432 is a use-after-free in the Linux kernel's IPv4 TCP handshake. One operation can free stored IPv4 options while another CPU is still reading them to construct a connection reply. The Linux kernel CNA rates the vulnerability Critical, with a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.8.
  • The vulnerable processing happens before an application authenticates a connection. A remote peer can trigger a race that discloses kernel memory, corrupts memory, or crashes the host. Anthropic reported a research exploit that executes commands as root on servers exposing a Multipath TCP (MPTCP) listener; this is not evidence of exploitation in the wild.
  • The Go Security Team warns that the underlying bug is not specific to MPTCP and that similar attacks may be possible without MPTCP listeners. Its guidance notes that Go programs enable MPTCP listeners by default on Linux from Go 1.24, subject to configuration. Disabling MPTCP is not a substitute for patching the kernel.
  • The upstream fix defers freeing the options until concurrent readers have finished. Distribution vendors backport the fix under their own package versions. Updating an application or rebuilding a container image alone does not patch the host kernel, and installing a new kernel does not by itself prove that the running kernel is fixed.

Why this needs attention

An unauthenticated remote attacker can reach the vulnerable Linux kernel code before application authentication. Researchers demonstrated root command execution against MPTCP listeners, and distribution-specific patch availability requires active review. Exploitation in the wild is not established in the reviewed sources.

Who should investigate

Organizations running an unpatched Linux kernel with IPv4 TCP networking enabled, particularly hosts accepting inbound connections. Review web servers, SSH endpoints, databases, load balancers, container hosts, and Kubernetes nodes. The upstream flaw dates to Linux 4.4; distribution kernels require vendor-specific backport checks. Prioritize exposed MPTCP listeners, including Go services that enable them by default, but do not assume hosts without MPTCP are unaffected.

What to do now

Check the running host kernel against your distribution's CVE advisory, apply its fixed kernel, and complete the required reboot or vendor-supported activation procedure. Verify that the fix is active, including on container hosts and Kubernetes nodes.

  1. Inventory running Linux kernels and reachable IPv4 TCP services, including container hosts, Kubernetes nodes, appliances, and managed infrastructure.
  2. Use the relevant distribution or platform vendor's advisory to determine affected builds, backported fixes, and the supported update and activation procedure.
  3. Prioritize internet-facing hosts and MPTCP listeners. Review internal and container-network exposure too; absence of MPTCP does not establish that a host is safe.
  4. Where a patch cannot yet be applied, consult vendor mitigation guidance. Red Hat describes IPv4-option filtering as exposure reduction, not complete prevention; verify compatibility with your network and workloads.

Assess your exposure with an agent

Copy this prompt into an agent with access to your infrastructure. It asks for an evidence-based assessment of affected systems, exposure, and gaps that need investigation.

Assess whether the infrastructure available to you is affected by CVE-2026-98432, the Linux IPv4 TCP use-after-free vulnerability. Perform a read-only assessment within your authorized access. Do not send exploit packets, stress-test listeners, change firewall rules, or reboot systems.

1. Verify the current Linux CVE record at https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-98432 and the relevant distribution or platform vendor advisories. Consult https://access.redhat.com/security/vulnerabilities/RHSB-2026-016 and the Go Security Team's applicability guidance at https://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2026/10/30/1 where relevant. Establish affected and fixed builds, including vendor backports. Cite sources and retrieval dates; flag anything you cannot verify.

2. Inventory accessible Linux hosts, virtual machines, container hosts, Kubernetes nodes, appliances, and managed platforms. Record the asset, environment, owner where known, distribution, running kernel release/build, installed kernel packages, and any verified livepatch status. Use read-only evidence such as uname -r, uname -v, package metadata, and platform inventory. Match vendor fixes to the running kernel, not merely an installed update or an image tag. Containers share their host's kernel: rebuilding an application image does not patch it. If host access is unavailable, record that gap and request confirmation from the operator or provider.

3. Identify internet-facing and internal IPv4 TCP listeners and the paths that can reach them, including direct-origin access, load balancers, and container networks. Check MPTCP listeners and configuration in relevant network namespaces using read-only inspection such as ss -Mlnp and sysctl net.mptcp.enabled where supported. Review Go services and their MPTCP settings. An enabled sysctl alone does not prove that an MPTCP listener exists; an empty result without sufficient access does not establish absence across the host. Prioritize exposed MPTCP listeners, but do not classify a kernel as unaffected simply because MPTCP is disabled or no such listener was found.

4. Assess network-layer compensating controls separately from kernel patch status. Where accessible, inspect filtering of IPv4 TCP packets carrying IP options and whether alternate or container-network paths bypass it. Do not confuse IPv4 options with TCP options or claim that filtering fully fixes the vulnerability. HTTP WAF rules do not address this pre-HTTP TCP-handshake flaw. A proxy or firewall configuration alone does not establish that every path to the host is protected.

Return a concise summary and a table: asset/host | running kernel/build | assessment (affected, fixed, not applicable, or unknown) | IPv4/MPTCP exposure | supporting evidence | next action. Separate kernel applicability from network reachability. Prioritize affected internet-facing systems, identify installed-but-not-active fixes, and link to current vendor remediation and activation guidance. List unassessed systems and the exact evidence or access needed to resolve unknowns. Distinguish a demonstrated research exploit from exploitation in the wild; do not infer absence of compromise from patch status or a lack of alerts. Propose verification steps without applying changes, and limit conclusions to the scope actually assessed.

Find more information and resources at https://radar.cloudflare.com/security/zero-wire/linux-ipv4-tcp-use-after-free

Cloudflare coverage

Product coverage

Magic Transit customers can use Cloudflare Network Firewall to reduce exposure by filtering IPv4 TCP packets carrying IP options before they reach their infrastructure. Coverage depends on routing and firewall configuration and does not replace kernel patching.

Service status

Cloudflare was not impacted by this vulnerability.

Evidence and sources

CVE record

The Linux kernel CNA documents the race condition, upstream affected and fixed branches, and Critical CVSS 3.1 severity of 9.8. Distribution package versions must be checked against vendor advisories.

  • CVE-2026-98432

Vendor advisory

Red Hat describes unauthenticated remote code execution potential and broad IPv4 TCP exposure. Its interim filtering guidance reduces exposure but does not replace kernel updates.

  • Red Hat RHSB-2026-016

Runtime applicability

The Go Security Team explains MPTCP listener defaults and warns that systems without MPTCP listeners may still be vulnerable to similar attacks.

  • Go Security Team advisory

Exploit evidence

Anthropic reports a working research exploit against Linux servers with MPTCP listeners. The reviewed sources do not establish exploitation in the wild.

  • Anthropic research disclosure

CISA KEV

CVE-2026-98432 was not present in the CISA KEV feed retrieved on 2 November 2026 (catalog version 2026.10.30). Absence from KEV is not evidence that exploitation cannot occur.

  • CISA KEV catalog

Product coverage

Magic Transit includes Cloudflare Network Firewall. Its IPv4 header-length field supports filtering packets carrying IP options; this is a configurable exposure-reduction capability, not a verified default-on CVE-specific mitigation.

  • Magic Transit network filtering
  • Cloudflare Network Firewall fields

Technical analysis and distribution tracking

Atlas provides a technical explanation and links to distribution patch trackers. Its 1 November update reports RHEL fixes and outstanding updates elsewhere; consult each vendor for current availability.

  • Atlas Linux IPv4 TCP analysis

item.title: php2shell
item.dc:creator: Cloudforce One
item.description: Prioritize patching. Cloudflare reported that PHP CTF submissions helped harden php2shell WAF protections and create new detections. Patch the PHP runtime using the original security advisory and separately review PHP's session upload progress advisory for CVE-2026-115560. Keep compensating controls in place while patching, and ask managed hosting providers to confirm each issue's status.
item.content:encoded:
Prioritize patching · Last checked Nov 2, 2026

Two PHP runtime flaws can allow unauthenticated code execution, data exposure, or crashes. A related follow-up, CVE-2026-115560, adds a configuration-dependent session upload progress RCE vector.

Update chronology

  • Oct 30, 2026: Cloudflare reported that PHP CTF submissions helped harden php2shell WAF protections and create new detections.
  • Oct 27, 2026: Cloudflare launched its PHP Capture the Flag challenge to test WAF protections through the Bug Bounty program.
  • Oct 26, 2026: CISA added the original CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 vulnerabilities to KEV.
  • Oct 23, 2026: PHP published its session upload progress informational advisory for the related CVE-2026-115560, describing unusual serializer configuration prerequisites and recommending disabling upload progress pending the next regular bugfix release.
  • Oct 21, 2026: PHP and Cloudflare published their initial security and mitigation guidance for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.

What happened

  • php2shell is the name used for two PHP runtime vulnerabilities disclosed on 21 October: CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. They affect how PHP manages memory when processing an HTTP request fails unexpectedly, including when memory is exhausted.
  • Normally PHP allocates memory to process a request and safely releases it when work finishes. In these cases, an error can interrupt that process. PHP may then use internal data that was never fully initialized, or later follow references to memory that has already been released.
  • An attacker can send specially crafted HTTP traffic to trigger those conditions. The result can range from a crashed PHP process to information disclosure or attacker-controlled code execution. Updating website code or a plugin alone does not fix the runtime defect.
  • Related follow-up: CVE-2026-115560. PHP's 23 October informational advisory describes an additional RCE vector involving session upload progress. It requires upload progress to remain enabled and the application to switch its session serializer from php_binary or php_serialize to php at runtime, using ini_set() before session_start(). The advisory recommends disabling session upload progress pending the next regular bugfix release; applications that never change the serializer at runtime can keep the feature enabled. Patching the original php2shell vulnerabilities does not establish that this follow-up is addressed.
  • CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are listed in CISA KEV as known exploited. Exploitation of CVE-2026-115560 is not established in the reviewed sources.

Why this needs attention

CISA has listed CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 as known exploited. The related CVE-2026-115560 requires a separate session-configuration assessment; exploitation of that follow-up is not established in the reviewed sources. These PHP runtime issues require attention beyond application-code or plugin updates.

Who should investigate

Teams running PHP 5.4 or later should review the original runtime vulnerabilities, including applications built on WordPress, Magento, and other PHP frameworks. The related CVE-2026-115560 has narrower prerequisites: session upload progress is enabled, and application code changes session.serialize_handler from php_binary or php_serialize to php at runtime before session_start(). Assess each CVE against its own advisory.

What to do now

Patch the PHP runtime using the original security advisory and separately review PHP's session upload progress advisory for CVE-2026-115560. Keep compensating controls in place while patching, and ask managed hosting providers to confirm each issue's status.

  1. Identify internet-facing applications running PHP and establish their runtime version.
  2. Apply the PHP project’s security update, including through managed hosting providers.
  3. Review the session upload progress advisory for CVE-2026-115560 separately, including application serializer changes and any vendor updates that supersede its interim guidance.
  4. Review logs and incident-response processes for suspicious PHP request activity.
  5. Keep edge mitigations enabled while the update is being deployed.

Assess your exposure with an agent

Copy this prompt into an agent with access to your infrastructure. It asks for an evidence-based assessment of affected systems, exposure, and gaps that need investigation.

Assess whether the infrastructure available to you is affected by the original php2shell vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) and the related session upload progress issue CVE-2026-115560. Perform a read-only assessment within your authorized access. Do not send exploit payloads, trigger memory exhaustion, or change systems.

1. Verify the current PHP advisories at https://www.php.net/archive/2026.php#2026-10-21-5 and https://www.php.net/archive/2026.php#2026-10-23-1, along with any superseding PHP, operating-system, or hosting-provider advisories. Establish affected and fixed releases or interim guidance for each CVE, including vendor backports. Cite sources and retrieval dates; flag anything you cannot verify. Report applicability, patch status, and exploitation evidence separately for each of the three CVEs. Do not extend CISA KEV evidence for the original two vulnerabilities to CVE-2026-115560.

2. Inventory PHP across accessible hosts, containers, Kubernetes workloads, images, and managed hosting, including WordPress, Magento, and other PHP applications. Record the service, environment, owner where known, runtime/package version, and image digest or build identity. Distinguish running deployments from repository declarations and unused images. Check the PHP runtime actually serving requests (for example PHP-FPM or Apache), not just the CLI version. If updates were installed, verify that running processes and replicas use the updated build.

3. Compare each deployed runtime against authoritative advisories for the original two CVEs. Do not treat an older version string as vulnerable if the vendor documents a backported fix, or an updated application/plugin as evidence that PHP itself is patched. Identify internet-facing and internal request paths, including origins reachable directly. Record access gaps; absence of PHP in one repository does not establish its absence across the infrastructure.

4. Assess CVE-2026-115560 separately. Inspect effective session.upload_progress.enabled and session.serialize_handler configuration, and application code that uses ini_set() to switch the serializer from php_binary or php_serialize to php before session_start(). Verify the relevant request-handling configuration rather than relying on CLI defaults. If configuration or code is inaccessible, report unknown. Follow current vendor guidance to distinguish fixed, mitigated, and not-applicable deployments; do not assume that updates for the original two CVEs also resolve this follow-up. Report findings without changing settings.

5. Report WAF or other compensating controls separately from runtime patch status. Where configuration is accessible, check whether relevant traffic is proxied, applicable rules are enabled in Block, and exceptions or bypass paths exist. Verify coverage for each CVE rather than assuming one php2shell rule covers every path. A WAF rule, blocked attack, or lack of alerts does not prove that the runtime is patched or that compromise has not occurred.

Return a concise summary and a table: asset/service | deployed runtime/build | assessment per CVE (affected, fixed, not applicable, or unknown) | compensating controls | exposure | supporting evidence | next action. Prioritize affected internet-facing services. List unassessed systems and the exact evidence or access needed to resolve unknowns. Link to current vendor remediation guidance and propose verification steps without applying changes. Do not conclude that the entire infrastructure is unaffected unless the assessed scope supports that conclusion.

Find more information and resources at https://radar.cloudflare.com/security/zero-wire/php2shell

Cloudflare coverage

Product coverage

Cloudflare has WAF rules for known php2shell exploit patterns. They are a compensating control, not a fix for the vulnerable PHP runtime.

Review your WAF configuration to determine whether you are protected.

  • Paid plans
  • Free plans

Service status

No impact to Cloudflare identified from the original php2shell vulnerabilities; monitoring continues.

Evidence and sources

Vendor advisory

Authoritative affected-version and remediation guidance for the original CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 vulnerabilities.

  • PHP security advisory

Related session upload progress advisory

PHP's 23 October informational advisory covers CVE-2026-115560, its unusual session serializer prerequisites, and interim mitigation. It explicitly connects this guidance to a mitigation already listed for CVE-2026-109619; the follow-up needs a separate applicability and remediation assessment.

  • PHP session upload progress advisory (CVE-2026-115560)

CVE records

Identifiers for the two original php2shell vulnerabilities and the related session upload progress follow-up.

  • CVE-2026-109618
  • CVE-2026-109619
  • CVE-2026-115560

CISA KEV

CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 were added to CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog on 26 October 2026. This statement does not extend to CVE-2026-115560. CISA's entries for the original two CVEs say ransomware use is unknown and require forensic triage for covered federal agencies.

  • CISA KEV catalog

Coordinated disclosure and research

Cloudflare's disclosure account identifies the PHP Foundation, Calif.io, Wiz, OpenAI, and Quarkslab as coordination participants.

  • Cloudflare php2shell research
  • PHP Foundation disclosure note

Exploit evidence

Cloudflare reported observing attack traffic targeting customers for the original php2shell vulnerabilities. This is evidence of observed attempts, not a claim about a particular organization's compromise. Exploitation of the related CVE-2026-115560 is not established in the reviewed sources.

  • Cloudflare observed-activity report

Protection testing

Cloudflare's PHP Capture the Flag challenge invites researchers to test php2shell WAF protections in a designated sandbox under its Bug Bounty program. The 30 October update reports that submissions helped harden existing protections and create new detections. WAF protections do not replace PHP updates.

  • Introducing the Cloudflare PHP Capture the Flag challenge

item.title: eMudhra certificate compromise
item.dc:creator: Cloudforce One
item.description: Review trust settings. Cloudflare published follow-up research on forged certificates, client patching progress, and the limitations of its measurements. Identify systems that rely on the affected certificate chain, update trust stores and client software according to the official response, and review customer-managed origins, mutual TLS, and container images.
item.content:encoded:
Review trust settings · Last checked Nov 2, 2026

Eight compromised eMudhra intermediate certificates could enable server impersonation and interception of traffic where affected certificates remain trusted.

Update chronology

  • Oct 30, 2026: Cloudflare published follow-up research on forged certificates, client patching progress, and the limitations of its measurements.
  • Oct 21, 2026: Cloudflare updated its response and customer action table.
  • Oct 20, 2026: Cloudflare published the certificate-compromise response and recommended customer actions.

What happened

  • A compromise of intermediate certificate authorities can allow an attacker holding a fraudulent but trusted certificate to impersonate a service or intercept traffic. The risk depends on whether a client or service still trusts the affected intermediates.
  • This is a certificate-trust incident, not a CVE-scored software vulnerability. It requires a different response: review trust stores and client software as well as applications and infrastructure that perform certificate validation.
  • Cloudflare's follow-up reports certificates forged using the weak keys and continued acceptance of affected chains among sampled clients. Forged certificates alone do not establish successful interception. The client measurements come from challenge-page traffic with a skewed, bot-heavy sample; they are not an Internet-wide patch-rate estimate.

Why this needs attention

Compromised intermediate certificates can affect how clients and services validate remote identities. The follow-up research documents forged certificates and continued acceptance of affected chains in sampled clients. Customer-managed clients, origins, mutual TLS deployments, and container images may still require action.

Who should investigate

Services and applications that trust the affected eMudhra intermediate certificates, including customer-managed TLS trust stores, clients, origins, mutual TLS configurations, and container images. This concerns certificate authentication, not a break in TLS encryption.

What to do now

Identify systems that rely on the affected certificate chain, update trust stores and client software according to the official response, and review customer-managed origins, mutual TLS, and container images.

  1. Identify customer-managed clients, origins, mutual TLS configurations, and container images that may trust the affected intermediates.
  2. Apply the product-specific client and trust-store updates in the official response.
  3. Review certificate-validation and outbound HTTPS paths that are not managed by Cloudflare.

Cloudflare coverage

Product coverage

No WAF rules are applicable to this certificate-trust incident.

Service status

As reported on 30 October, all high-priority Cloudflare systems were patched; lower-impact remediation remained in progress.

Evidence and sources

Incident response

Cloudflare's response contains the affected-certificate context and a customer action table by product.

  • Cloudflare eMudhra certificate-compromise response

Product guidance

Relevant product documentation for customer-managed trust and outbound HTTPS paths.

  • cloudflared releases
  • Gateway traffic policies
  • Container HTTPS egress interception

CVE status

No CVE was cited for this certificate compromise. It is tracked as a security incident rather than a software vulnerability.

Exploitation and patching research

Cloudflare's follow-up documents forged certificates and measurements of client acceptance of compromised chains. Certificate forgery is not proof of successful interception, and the challenge-page sample is skewed by bot traffic and limited to clients executing JavaScript.

  • 4 real? Tracking exploitation and patching of eMudhra's weak keys

item.title: node2shell
item.dc:creator: Cloudforce One
item.description: Assess your exposure. Cloudflare documented two WAF rules and their default Log action. Identify every Brotli decoder in running runtimes, dependencies, and container images, then use each vendor's security guidance to update or otherwise remove the vulnerable decoder.
item.content:encoded:
Assess your exposure · Last checked Oct 25, 2026

CVE-2026-111497 is a memory-corruption flaw in the shared Brotli decoder. Any service that decompresses attacker-controlled Brotli, in a request or an HTTP response, can be exposed.

Update chronology

  • Oct 25, 2026: Cloudflare documented two WAF rules and their default Log action.
  • Oct 21, 2026: Node.js published security-release guidance for the vulnerability.

What happened

  • node2shell is the early name for CVE-2026-111497, an out-of-bounds write in the Brotli decoder. The decoder can mistake a malformed block switch for a temporary lack of input, continue appending bytes to a small internal buffer, and corrupt process memory.
  • The name can be misleading: the flaw is in a widely reused Brotli library, not in Node.js alone. It can reach applications through runtimes, HTTP clients, framework middleware, and container images that bundle or install the decoder.
  • In Node.js, applications can reach the decoder through node:zlib or Brotli-aware request middleware. Node.js built-in fetch is powered by Undici and automatically handles Brotli responses, so server-side URL fetches and remote-image features require review too. Gzip, Deflate, and Zstd are not the decoder affected by this CVE. The cited sources do not establish active exploitation.

Why this needs attention

The risk extends beyond Node.js deployments, and affected runtime and server-side fetch paths require active assessment. Active exploitation is not established in the reviewed sources, but scope and remediation guidance are still developing.

Who should investigate

Teams should investigate runtimes, HTTP clients, libraries, and container images that include a vulnerable Brotli decoder. For Node.js, review direct node:zlib use, Brotli-inflating request middleware, and server-side fetches of untrusted URLs. Next.js remote image optimization is a documented server-side response path.

What to do now

Identify every Brotli decoder in running runtimes, dependencies, and container images, then use each vendor's security guidance to update or otherwise remove the vulnerable decoder.

  1. Inventory runtimes, HTTP libraries, dependencies, and container images that provide Brotli decoding.
  2. Apply the security update or vendor guidance for every affected component, then rebuild and redeploy affected workloads.
  3. Prioritize inbound Brotli request handling and outbound fetch, webhook, crawler, URL-preview, proxy, and remote-image features that retrieve untrusted responses.

Cloudflare coverage

Product coverage

Cloudflare has WAF rules for documented Node2Shell request patterns. They default to Log and customers must configure them to Block if blocking mitigation is needed.

Review your WAF configuration to determine whether you are protected.

  • Paid plans

Service status

No impact; Brotli is not currently used in Cloudflare infrastructure.

Evidence and sources

Vendor advisory

Authoritative Node.js remediation guidance and affected-release information.

  • Node.js security advisory

CVE record

Canonical identifier for the Brotli decoder flaw.

  • CVE-2026-111497

CISA KEV

KEV inclusion was not established in the sources reviewed for this snapshot.

  • CISA KEV catalog

Technical research

Independent research describes the shared-library and HTTP attack-path context beyond Node.js deployments.

  • Aikido Node2Shell research

Exploit evidence

The sources reviewed do not establish active exploitation.

Read the briefing

item.title: Citrix NetScaler command execution
item.dc:creator: Cloudforce One
item.description: Prioritize patching. Cloudflare published defense-in-depth guidance while distinguishing web authentication from other gateway traffic. Use Citrix's bulletin to identify and update affected appliances. Treat suspected compromise separately from patching, and review exposed gateway services and incident-response guidance.
item.content:encoded:
Prioritize patching · Last checked Oct 19, 2026

An unauthenticated attacker can execute commands on affected NetScaler ADC and Gateway appliances, including default configurations.

Update chronology

  • Oct 19, 2026: Cloudflare published defense-in-depth guidance while distinguishing web authentication from other gateway traffic.
  • Oct 1, 2026: Cloudflare documented a CVE-specific managed WAF rule with a default Block action.

What happened

  • CVE-2026-88771 is an unauthenticated command-execution issue in Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway appliances. Citrix reports exploitation on deployments that have not been mitigated.
  • The issue can affect default configurations and occurs before the authentication boundary, so exposure review should not be limited to appliances with optional features enabled.
  • Patching remains necessary. WAF and access controls can reduce exposure of applicable web authentication traffic but do not automatically protect other gateway services, including DTLS listeners.

Why this needs attention

Citrix reports exploitation on unmitigated deployments, and the affected gateway can be compromised before sign-in. Every customer-managed NetScaler ADC or Gateway appliance, including default configurations, needs prompt review.

Who should investigate

Organizations operating customer-managed Citrix NetScaler ADC or Gateway appliances on affected releases. CVE-2026-88771 requires no additional feature to be enabled.

What to do now

Use Citrix's bulletin to identify and update affected appliances. Treat suspected compromise separately from patching, and review exposed gateway services and incident-response guidance.

  1. Inventory all customer-managed NetScaler ADC and Gateway appliances, including internet-facing and default configurations.
  2. Apply Citrix remediation and investigate any suspected compromise using the vendor's incident-response guidance.
  3. Review whether alternate hostnames, direct-origin paths, or non-HTTP gateway services bypass protective controls.

Cloudflare coverage

Product coverage

Cloudflare has a WAF rule for the documented NetScaler HTTP exploit path.

Review your WAF configuration to determine whether you are protected.

  • Paid plans

Service status

No impact on Cloudflare infrastructure.

Evidence and sources

Vendor advisory

Citrix's security bulletin provides affected-release, remediation, and exploitation context.

  • Citrix CTX697096
  • Citrix suspected-compromise guidance

CVE record

Canonical identifier for this NetScaler command-execution issue.

  • CVE-2026-88771

Technical guidance

Cloudflare's response distinguishes WAF coverage from Access and restricted-origin exposure reduction.

  • Cloudflare NetScaler guidance
  • Emergency WAF release

Exploit evidence

Citrix reports exploitation on unmitigated deployments.

  • Citrix security bulletin

item.title: WordPress SQL injection and RCE
item.dc:creator: Cloudforce One
item.description: Update affected systems. Cloudflare updated its response with vulnerability and remediation guidance. Confirm WordPress update status against the vendor release and patch guidance. Keep any compensating controls in place while remediation is completed.
item.content:encoded:
Update affected systems · Last checked Jul 20, 2026

Two related WordPress flaws can expose database contents and allow unauthenticated code execution through distinct SQL-injection and REST API attack paths.

Update chronology

  • Jul 20, 2026: Cloudflare updated its response with vulnerability and remediation guidance.
  • Jul 17, 2026: WordPress published the security release and Cloudflare published its WAF response.

What happened

  • CVE-2026-60137 is a SQL-injection issue and CVE-2026-63030 is an unauthenticated code-execution issue associated with a REST API attack path. Their affected versions and conditions differ.
  • The cited WordPress release provides the authoritative remediation and backport information. The sources reviewed for this reference record did not establish active exploitation.
  • Managed WAF rules can mitigate known requests, but do not repair WordPress installations or replace vendor updates.

Why it remains relevant

Vendor remediation and applicability guidance are stable, and active exploitation was not established in the cited sources. The record remains relevant to organizations that have not verified their WordPress update state.

Who should investigate

Organizations operating WordPress sites. The two issues have different version and configuration conditions; the WordPress security release is authoritative for applicability.

What to do now

Confirm WordPress update status against the vendor release and patch guidance. Keep any compensating controls in place while remediation is completed.

  1. Identify WordPress sites and compare their versions with the WordPress security release.
  2. Apply the vendor update or backport guidance for each affected deployment.
  3. Confirm that internet-facing WordPress traffic follows the intended security controls during remediation.

Cloudflare coverage

Product coverage

Cloudflare has WAF rules for documented WordPress exploit paths. They are a compensating control, not a replacement for updating WordPress.

Review your WAF configuration to determine whether you are protected.

  • Paid plans

Service status

No impact to Cloudflare. We do not use WordPress on our infrastructure.

Evidence and sources

Vendor advisory

WordPress's release contains security-update and backport guidance for both issues.

  • WordPress 7.0.2 security release

CVE records

Canonical identifiers for the SQL-injection and code-execution paths.

  • CVE-2026-60137
  • CVE-2026-63030

Technical research

Cloudflare's response documents the two WAF rules and their respective attack paths.

  • Cloudflare WordPress response

Exploit evidence

Active exploitation was not established in the cited WordPress release or Cloudflare response.

Read the briefing · Read the blog post
